name: David Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fencing, tools, feed and fasteners for Prairie Farm and Hardware Supply, which serves farms and hardware shops across three counties. My father had a hardware store in Millbrook, and I ran it with him until it closed, so I came to the buying desk only three years ago and I'm still learning it. My day is the phone, a price book that's older than some of my colleagues, and the farmers who call when the wire's late. I like talking to men who actually use what I buy. I don't like the new order screens one bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because a lot of it is noise. Folks have been telling me for years that a computer will do my job, and I'm still here picking up the phone and getting the fence wire to the farm by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm more worried about money than machines. The store closing took the family savings, and we've got about three months in the bank now. Prairie's steady, but I'm the junior, and a firm that's steady can still decide to be steadier with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the way I always have. I'd keep going to church on Sundays, keep my head down and my price book up to date, and keep ringing my farmers by name. I'd put 100 pounds a month aside, and no more spending on anything I don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled enough, but never easy. I've had a business go under once, and you don't forget the feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your father's store closing. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big box stores opened out on the highway and my father couldn't match their prices. He kept the doors open two years longer than he should have, and it cost him his savings and a bit of his health. I watch every contract at Prairie with that in my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Prairie decided to push the screen system harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, because a man has to work. But I'd do it badly and slowly, and I'd tell my boss Walt the truth about it. I won't pretend I like it.

say: I'd say it's mostly **noise**; I'm still picking up the phone and getting wire to farms.
I'd tell folks I'll keep doing what **works**.
think: I'm more worried about **money** than machines since the store closing took our savings.
A steady firm can still become steadier with **fewer people**.
do: Keep ringing my farmers **by name** and my price book up to date.
Put aside **100 pounds** a month and stop spending on extras.
feel: **Settled** enough, but never easy after a business going under.
S0.quote: I've had a business go under once, and you don't forget the feeling.
fieldNote: His wariness comes from the **family store** closing, not from AI.
Still reads every contract with that **memory** in mind.
Would obey the screen system but say **honestly** that he doesn't like it.

steps.text: Keep phoning my regular farm customers every week
Put 100 pounds a month into the savings account
Stop all spending on things we don't need

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they've got to be careful what they wish for. I'd tell the men at church that a country that forgets how to make and fix things is a poorer country, however clever its screens get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my days are numbered, and I'm not too proud to say so. Prairie's order system suggests stock and a new buyer is learning it fast. I'm the slow one, and I'm 58, and the manager sees that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my hardest, since a hard worker is harder to cut. I'd ask Walt if I could do more of the farm visits, since that's where I'm useful. And I'd talk with my brother-in-law Ray about doing fencing jobs on weekends if I get let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a little angry too. I've worked every day of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the buying would a computer do better than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The comparing of prices and the checking of invoices, the screen does it in no time and never complains. What a screen can't do is know that old Mr Pruitt, one of my farm customers, will pay late but always pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the buying desk was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies and the people who build these things and never get their hands dirty. And politicians who say retrain, but never say who pays for the training. I don't blame Walt, he's just caught in it.

say: I'd say they should be careful what they **wish for**.
I'd tell the church men a country that forgets how to **fix things** is poorer.
think: My days are **numbered** and I'm the slow one at 58.
The manager can see that I'm slower on the **new system**.
do: Work harder and ask Walt for more **farm visits**.
Talk to my brother-in-law Ray about **weekend fencing** jobs.
feel: **Anxious** and a little angry; I've worked every day of my life.
S1.quote: What a screen can't do is know that old Mr Pruitt, one of my farm customers, will pay late but always pays.
fieldNote: Plans around **hands-on work** with his brother-in-law.
Anger is aimed at **big companies** and politicians, not his boss.
Defines his worth by **hard work** and local knowledge.

steps.text: Ask Walt to give me more farm visits
Do weekend fencing jobs with my brother-in-law Ray
Wait to see which buyers Prairie keeps this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got two years to get ready, and nobody's getting ready. I'd tell the church men we'd better look after each other, because the government won't do it in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone within two years and I'd be 60, with a wife and about three months' savings. I'd say I feel like my father felt when the big stores came, only quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Ray first and see if we could set up a proper fencing and farm repairs business. We'd buy a second trailer and tools, using what's in the bank. I'd also ask Pastor Dan about the church's emergency fund, which I hate to do but would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't sleep. I know it's been coming for years, but I thought I'd be gone before it landed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn for help, beyond family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church mostly, and the farmers I've known twenty years, who'd give me work before a stranger. I hate asking. I've been giving to the church fund every Sunday for thirty years, and I'd take what I put in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Rosa works at the thrift shop. What would she say to you about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa'd say stop frowning and do what we've always done: work, pray and put something by. She'd be worried herself, though. Her wage at the thrift shop is small.

say: I'd say we have two years and **nobody** is getting ready.
I'd tell the church men to look after **each other**.
think: My job is gone in two years and I'd be **60** with three months' savings.
I feel like my father did when the big stores came, only **quicker**.
do: Ring Ray and set up a proper **fencing and farm repairs** business.
Ask Pastor Dan about the church's **emergency fund**.
feel: **Frightened** and sleepless; I thought I'd be gone before it landed.
S2.quote: I've been giving to the church fund every Sunday for thirty years, and I'd take what I put in.
fieldNote: The **echo** of his father's store drives the fear.
His plan is hands-on: **repairs** and fencing, using tools and savings.
Reluctant to ask for **help** but sees it as earned.

steps.text: Set up a fencing and farm repairs business with Ray
Buy a second trailer and fencing tools
Ask Pastor Dan about the church's emergency fund
Look for farm supply counter work in nearby towns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something to build on. I'd tell the men at church to teach their sons a trade, because trades are what hold a place together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little easier. I'd be 63, three or four years from the finish line, and I could work out how to get there. I still think the desk will go, but I'd have time to get the repair business going on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at Prairie as long as they'll have me. Meanwhile I'd start the fencing work part-time, and save 200 pounds a month toward a decent trailer and tools. I'd help my son Mateo get his apprenticeship finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier to breathe. Still not easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the five year gap change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo is an apprentice electrician, and I'd tell him he's lucky. Robots are three years slower to reach hands-on work, and people always need a wire fixed in a wet cellar. I'd say stay with the trade, and keep some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sons about their own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the screen can add numbers, but it can't stand in a barn and tell a man his fence is crooked. I want them both to know how to do a real job.

say: I'd say five years is something to **build** on.
I'd tell the men at church to teach their sons a **trade**.
think: I'd be **63**, three or four years from the finish line, with time to plan.
I still think the desk will go, but I'd have time to start the **repair business**.
do: Work at Prairie as long as they will have me and start **fencing** part-time.
Save **200 pounds** a month for a trailer and tools.
feel: **Easier** to breathe, but still not easy.
S3.quote: The screen can add numbers, but it can't stand in a barn and tell a man his fence is crooked.
fieldNote: Uses the **extra years** to build a trade side-business.
Cares most that his **sons** learn a real job.
Gets his **hope** from hands-on work, not from tools.

steps.text: Start part-time fencing jobs on Saturdays
Save 200 pounds a month for a trailer and tools
Help my son Mateo finish his electrician apprenticeship
Keep buying at Prairie for as long as they'll have me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and in that time people always find a new way. I'd say we'll adjust, because we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For myself, I'd be 68, and I'd have retired quietly. My worry is for my children and grandchildren, who'd be starting families into it. I'd pray on that more than I'd worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65 or 66, if my knees allow. I'd save up to six months and help with the grandchildren's schooling where I can. And I'd get the repair business humming as a hobby for the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly peaceful. I'd feel it for the young ones, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is past your pension age. What would your worries be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My real fear would be what a world with no need for people's work does to a man's pride. I've known men who retired and just faded. Work gives you your place, and I wouldn't want that gone for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope people remember about your generation of workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we showed up and did a day's work, and we taught the young ones to do the same. That's enough for a headstone.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people always find a **new way**.
I'd say we'll **adjust**, because we always have.
think: My worry is for my children and **grandchildren**, who would be raising families into it.
do: Work until **65 or 66** if my knees allow.
Save up to **six months** and help with the grandchildren's schooling.
feel: Fairly **peaceful**, though I'd feel it for the young ones.
S4.quote: Work gives you your place, and I wouldn't want that gone for everyone.
fieldNote: Calm for himself but worried about **purpose** when work disappears.
Uses faith and **family** to frame the future, and treats work as the thing that gives a person a place.

steps.text: Keep working at Prairie until I'm 65 or 66
Build savings to six months of expenses
Help pay for my grandchildren's schooling

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, because it's the same thing that happened to my father and the store, only faster, and I'd be 60 with three months in the bank. What would help is work that needs hands, a place in the community, and a chance to learn without being laughed at.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against progress. We just remember who paid last time the clever ideas went wrong, and it wasn't the clever people.

headlineQuote: We just remember who paid last time the clever ideas went wrong, and it wasn't the clever people.
portrait: David is a **58-year-old** junior buyer at a farm and hardware supplier, after his family's store closed.
He has about **three months** saved, a wife Rosa at a thrift shop, and an apprentice son.
Traditional in outlook and **resistant** to technology, he has never used AI and relies on local trust.
His fear is shaped by the **store closing**: money worries come first, machines second.
His answer is hands-on: **fencing work** with his brother-in-law, church support and the trades.
biggestWorry: The **two year** picture, which he sees as his father's story happening faster.
whatWouldHelp: Work that needs **hands**, community support and a chance to learn without ridicule.
